In a DC motor, torque \( T \) is proportional to the product of armature current \( I_a \) and field flux \( \phi \):  
\[
T \propto \phi I_a
\]  
Power \( P \) is proportional to \( T \times \text{speed} \) (\( P = T \omega \)).  

When field flux is weakened for speed increase above base speed (with armature voltage constant), the motor’s back EMF \( E_b = k \phi N \) stays roughly constant (since \( E_b \approx V - I_a R_a \)), so  
\[
N \propto \frac{1}{\phi}
\]  
If \( I_a \) is kept at rated value, then torque \( T \propto \phi \) decreases as flux decreases.  
Thus \( T \propto 1/N \), so  
\[
P = T \cdot N \propto \text{constant}
\]  
This is **constant power drive**.  

- (B) constant torque drive is wrong — that happens with armature voltage control below base speed, not field weakening.  
- (C) variable power drive is wrong — field weakening yields approximately constant power if \( I_a \) is constant.  
- (D) none of the above is wrong because (A) is correct.  

Final answer: (A)
